## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_How long can a robot act on a remembered scene after it loses sight of it?_

A person hidden behind a storage rack can keep moving while the robot's map still shows an empty aisle. Forgetting the person loses a constraint on motion; preserving the last position indefinitely turns old evidence into false certainty. The engineer must retain useful state through brief sensing gaps while limiting how long it can support a decision. That limit depends on the motion the sensors cannot observe, the error already present, and the clearance the task can tolerate. A stored estimate must therefore carry both its physical age and the conditions under which its uncertainty remains bounded. The permission path needs that information in time to refuse motion whose evidence has expired. Spatial memory connects sensing to the causal boundary by preserving what an observation supports without extending its authority beyond the physical margin.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Specify a Scene Memory State record that carries evidence age, uncertainty growth, and consumer query budgets
- Set belief expiry from bounded uncertainty growth and the task's physical tolerance
- Compare spatial representations (3D Gaussian splatting, NeRFs, octrees, and hashed TSDF/ESDF grids) across the memory footprint vs. query latency frontier
- Design spatial updates that preserve evidence age and distinguish missing observations from verified free space
- Diagnose frozen transforms, phantom tracks, and unobservable drift that pass freshness and innovation checks

:::

## Spatial Belief Persistence and Representation {#sec-memory-preserving-belief}

A digital memory register can preserve a bit pattern indefinitely while the physical world it describes moves. As a warehouse mobile manipulator pivots away from the end of a storage rack, the rack uprights hide the cross aisle from the navigation camera, and whatever the vision backbone last detected there now survives only in memory. A person out of sight past the rack end can walk directly into the corridor that memory marks empty. Republishing that cached observation with a fresh software timestamp cannot restore the lost sensory evidence. Spatial memory must therefore carry the physical measurement epoch and an explicit uncertainty-growth law into every downstream motion-permission decision. The aisle stopping calculation so far covers a static obstacle at the declared clearance. A hidden approaching person changes that premise; the worked expiry calculation below shows why a separately qualified crossing control or an operating restriction is required.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Observation age and calibrated spatial covariances are generated in @sec-perception-observation-contract.
:::

A physical AI system cannot rely solely on instantaneous sensory observations or static KV-cache tensors. It requires a **belief**\index{Belief}, an estimate of physical state carried forward from historical sensory evidence, coupled explicitly to an expanding model of uncertainty.[^fn-mem-belief-state] Perception supplies a dated, calibrated observation (as established in @sec-perception-handoff). Spatial memory must determine how long that observation, combined with dynamic motion models, can continue to authorize physical action before epistemic uncertainty consumes the machine's remaining safety clearance.

[^fn-mem-belief-state]: **Belief state formulation**\index{State estimation!belief state}: In a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), a belief represents a probability distribution over latent states. A physical state interface additionally carries an error bound. Without the value, frame, evidence epoch, and applicable uncertainty model, a downstream optimizer cannot evaluate clearance during a sensor dropout.

As the second of the four proposal-side stages of Part III, between perception and intent, **spatial memory**\index{Spatial memory} carries geometric and physical state estimates forward across sensor dropouts, occlusions, and variable processing delays. It sits above the proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), so a remembered state can shape a proposal but cannot certify its own freshness; the permission path checks the age of the evidence against its own monotonic clock.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_sp.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Sense-Plan belief edge."}
*The Sense $\cap$ Plan belief interface: preserving spatial object state under line-of-sight occlusions.*
:::

A learned policy's context retains information according to an attention and storage budget. A person who disappears behind a pallet rack can be evicted from that context while still constraining the robot's motion. This **frustum amnesia** makes an internal attention cache an unsuitable sole record of physical state. Spatial memory instead preserves the entity, its last observation, and the uncertainty that grows while it remains hidden.

Externalizing that state also separates the consumers' work. A policy retrieves a compact **spatial attention working set** around its candidate route from the host-resident scene map. An isolated permission controller instead consumes a bounded local safety snapshot, qualified for its clearance queries and available in its own memory. That snapshot preserves the source evidence epochs, uncertainty, coverage, and validity region; copying it does not make it fresh. The full map need not fit on the permission controller, and the controller must not wait for a host query to complete before deciding whether existing motion remains admissible.

Internal memory integrity alone cannot establish physical geometric validity. To prevent a machine from acting on stale data, memory systems must treat expiry as an explicit interface event. Each belief carries a deadline, its invalidation horizon (derived in @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion), at which its declared error bound reaches the task's physical margin. At that deadline the belief stops supporting motion, and the permission path refuses any proposal that still depends on it and selects a feasible fallback.

A belief that must declare its own expiry has to travel with more than its value, so the first handoff question is what a consumer needs to evaluate a stored value after its sensor loses sight of the object.

## The Spatial Memory Handoff and State Invariants {#sec-memory-handoff}

A position vector arriving over an inter-process bus cannot identify the entity, quantity, or units it describes. The same numbers could denote a workpiece center in meters, a joint angle in radians, or a contact force in newtons. A consumer needs those distinctions before applying a control law; a meters-to-millimeters mismatch alone changes the interpreted displacement by a thousandfold. The spatial belief record therefore begins with entity identity, physical quantity, and measurement units, rather than relying on conventions hidden in the producing model or transport wrapper.

Specifying the quantity and units remains incomplete without binding the value to a concrete reference frame. Identical spatial coordinates describe entirely different physical realities depending on the origin and orientation of the coordinate system. A Cartesian position $[0.142, -0.051, 0.812]\text{ m}$ designates a point suspended in free space when evaluated in the robot base frame\index{Base frame}, but represents a point several hundred millimeters inside a rigid fixture when interpreted in the tool flange frame\index{Tool flange frame}. Because kinematic links flex, joints move, and coordinate transforms update at varying rates, a belief record must carry an explicit frame identifier. Carrying the frame allows the receiving node to look up the corresponding spatial transformation tree and project the stored geometry into the local frame required by the actuator, preventing the controller from acting on geometric misalignments caused by moving kinematic chains.

Geometry and identity describe physical state at a single moment, but spatial memory must also capture the temporal anchor of that state. The record carries the evidence epoch $t_0$ of the physical interaction or optical exposure that last constrained the estimate at the causal boundary. In distributed machine architectures, intermediate nodes often republish data, execute Kalman filter prediction steps, or run forward kinematic propagations to maintain high-rate control streams; none of these computational steps adds physical evidence. The evidence epoch must therefore pass unchanged through every republish, filter, and prediction stage, so that consumers measure the age of the information against the physical world rather than against the scheduling frequency of the local computer.

Generating this anchored belief relies on **multi-sensor state estimation**\index{State estimation!contract boundary}\index{Sensor fusion!informational contract}. An estimator combines asynchronous observations with a motion model to infer the state between measurements [@kalman1960new]. Consumers need the resulting state, its justified error model, and the physical evidence that constrains each relevant component. They do not need to reproduce the estimator. A prediction step advances the estimate epoch while its evidence continues aging; a fresh measurement renews only the state dimensions it actually constrains. The covariance propagation mechanics are collected in @sec-appendix-control-covariance. Here the engineering obligation is to expose bounded growth through occlusion and withdraw claims whose assumptions no longer hold.

Knowing the evidence epoch $t_0$ establishes elapsed time $\Delta t = t - t_0$, but elapsed time alone cannot determine whether a belief is valid for a given action. Two estimates of identical age diverge at different rates depending on physical constraints. The rack end itself is bolted to the floor, so its remembered position can remain useful while the machine's localization bound and the fixed-rack premise hold, whereas a person hidden behind it can move at walking speed and spend the same clearance in a few tens of milliseconds.

The minimum record fields necessary for a consumer to evaluate a stored state can be derived directly from the requirement to bound current error. Let $E(\Delta t)$ represent the upper bound of the discrepancy between the stored value and true physical state after an elapsed time $\Delta t = t - t_0$. If an estimator establishes a state at time $t_0$ with an initial uncertainty bound\index{Uncertainty bound} $E_0$, and external disturbances or unmodeled velocities cause the true state to diverge at a maximum rate $r$, the upper bound on error at current time $t$ obeys the linear expansion\index{Error expansion} $E(\Delta t) = E_0 + r\,\Delta t$. At the rack end, $E_0$ is the machine's localization error and $r$ is the walking speed of the person the rack may hide; @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion evaluates that law. Under the stochastic acceleration-noise model developed below, double integration produces cubic growth of position variance ($\propto t^3$). Omitting the initial bound or the dynamic growth terms leaves the consumer unable to compute $E(\Delta t)$, so an initial bound and an explicit expansion model are both structurally required fields of the record.

Expressing uncertainty through physical bounds and expansion rates distinguishes a physical AI belief from a probabilistic confidence score. An object detection network might output a class confidence of $0.94$, but that softmax score is not calibrated evidence (@sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities), and a downstream position controller cannot convert a unitless probability into a safe actuator displacement margin (i.e., how far the arm can physically move before risking a collision). A confidence score of $0.94$ provides no information about whether an obstacle boundary is uncertain by $2.0\text{ mm}$ or by $200\text{ mm}$, nor does it indicate how rapidly that boundary moves when occlusion occurs. A physical memory record must express its initial bound $E_0$ and expansion rate $r$ in concrete physical dimensions such as meters, radians, or newtons per second. Furthermore, these rates are valid only within a declared validity region, such as a maximum assumed acceleration or a verified contact friction coefficient. If physical operating conditions leave that region, the expansion rate no longer holds, and the belief record must be treated as invalid.

When the gripper finger approaches the latch-release slot, the consumer compares the belief's current error with the slot clearance. It converts the evidence epoch into its own clock, includes the clock-conversion bound, and evaluates the declared growth law at the time the state will be used. This is a continuing obligation during execution, not a one-time path-generation check. A new proposal whose evidence fails the check is refused without automatically revoking a still-valid active command. If the active motion itself depends on expiring evidence, the controller must begin a feasible fallback early enough that the response remains within the available clearance. The belief's expiry is a limit on supported motion, not a promise that an instantaneous stop is possible at that instant.

::: {#dfn-memory-spatial-belief-contract .callout-definition title="Scene memory state record"}

***Scene Memory State record***\index{Scene Memory State record!definition}\index{Spatial belief record!definition}\index{Belief record!definition} is the eighth contract in the volume's lineage. It binds identified physical quantities and map regions to a reference frame, hardware evidence epochs, estimate epochs, clock-conversion bounds, uncertainty-growth laws, operating validity regions, task expiries, provenance, and lifecycle status. Each consumer also receives a query-work limit appropriate to its deadline. The record makes these claims checkable; qualification must establish that they hold.

1.  **Significance**: Consumers can distinguish a useful prediction from fresh evidence and determine when its error exhausts the task clearance. The worked local collision interface allocates at most $2\ \mu\text{s}$ per query; that allocation is derived from its workload rather than imposed on every scene representation.
2.  **Distinction**: A belief record couples physical units and evidence age to an error-growth model. A classification score, map publication time, or transform value alone cannot supply that contract.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Waiting for an upstream publisher to announce expiry. If its thread hangs or its messages stop, the consumer must still age the evidence and enforce its own deadline.

:::

Evaluating the spatial belief record depends on calculating the elapsed time $\Delta t = t_{\text{now}} - t_0$ against physical reality. If the consumer cannot verify the exact physical instant when energy transduction occurred, the calculated error bound $E(\Delta t)$ becomes an unanchored fiction, mistaking software compute cycles for physical evidence. The estimate epoch and clock conversion named in the definition exist to protect that anchor, while provenance and lifecycle status, the record's remaining fields, are developed with the schema in @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema.

## State Epochs and Temporal Anchoring {#sec-memory-state-epoch}

A bounding box or 3D Gaussian pose emitted by a neural object detector describes where an entity was when photons struck the camera CMOS sensor, not where it is when the inference tensor arrives in memory. Every spatial claim refers to a specific physical instant, its **epoch**\index{Epoch}, and any state crossing a physical AI pipeline carries three distinct epochs before an actuator can fire. The **acquisition epoch**\index{Epoch!acquisition} ($t_0$) is the capture epoch of the observation contract (@sec-perception-observation-contract)—the observation's physical time reference, such as the exposure midpoint for the camera or the instant a hardware register latches an encoder count—which spatial memory anchors as its evidence epoch.[^fn-hw-timer-capture] Spatial memory adds the two epochs that follow it. The **estimate epoch**\index{Epoch!estimate} ($t_{\text{est}}$) marks the physical instant that the estimated state describes. A predictor can advance that instant beyond the last observation without obtaining new evidence; the time at which computation finishes is a separate scheduling fact. The **publication epoch**\index{Epoch!publication} ($t_{\text{pub}}$) marks the instant the serialized state record was committed to the transport bus or shared-memory ring buffer for dispatch to downstream consumers.

[^fn-hw-timer-capture]: **Hardware timer input-capture**\index{Hardware!timer input-capture}: Microcontroller timer input-capture channels latch counter values into dedicated shadow registers upon external signal transitions, bypassing operating system interrupt latency. Reading capture registers without atomic synchronization against timer overflow flags causes 16-bit counter aliasing, injecting artificial timestamp jumps equal to the rollover period ($65.5\text{ ms}$ on a $1\text{ MHz}$ timer). In downstream visual-inertial state estimation, this temporal discontinuity introduces false acceleration spikes that destabilize platform attitude filters.

Collapsing these three timestamps into one receipt or transmission timestamp destroys the physical anchor. This **publish-time stamping anti-pattern**\index{Publish-time stamping anti-pattern!definition} occurs when a wrapper stamps its output with the current software clock after exposure, transport, inference, and postprocessing have already elapsed. The receiver then sees a recent message containing old evidence. The age-as-displacement relation established in @sec-perception-photons-to-claims still applies throughout that pipeline. Publication time helps diagnose scheduling delay, but only acquisition time lets a motion consumer account for the world's change since the measurement.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Synchronized hardware timestamping across fieldbuses is established in @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses.
:::

Even when a system records true acquisition epochs, physical AI architectures rely on distributed processing nodes whose local oscillator clocks drift independently. The deployed clock-conversion protocol must establish an error bound under its stated load and fault conditions; a bus interface alone supplies no such guarantee. That temporal uncertainty becomes spatial uncertainty at the relative speed of whatever the record describes.[^fn-hw-ptp-canfd] The observation record of @sec-perception-observation-contract already carries this bound as its clock-conversion error, and a belief built from that observation keeps it. Every consumer adds the bound to the evidence age before judging freshness, and the error budget allocates the distance that bound covers at the record's relative speed alongside sensor resolution and structural deflection. In safety enforcement, downstream Control Barrier Functions treat this clock-synchronization uncertainty $\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$ as an irreducible temporal margin, inflating the required spatial barrier clearance by $d_{\text{sync}} = v_{\text{rel}} \epsilon_{\text{sync}}$ before granting motor torque authorization.

[^fn-hw-ptp-canfd]: **Fieldbus clock synchronization jitter**\index{Fieldbus!synchronization jitter}: CAN-FD bit-phase synchronization aligns bit sampling within a frame; it does not synchronize the distributed clocks that date physical observations. A shared evidence-time basis requires a specified clock-conversion protocol and a qualified bound on its offset and drift. PTP and EtherCAT Distributed Clocks provide synchronization mechanisms, but their names alone do not establish the deployed error bound. The allowed temporal error follows from the task's spatial allocation and relative velocity ($e_{\text{sync}} = v_{\text{rel}} \delta t$).

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-epoch-alignment
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ILLUSTRATIVE SAMPLING EPOCHS FOR FUSION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-state-epoch (three sensors latch at different epochs).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that fusing two observations requires projecting one across
# │          the gap between their acquisition epochs.
# │ Show:    tactile 12 ms, camera 18.5 ms, encoders 21 ms; camera-to-encoder
# │          gap 2.5 ms.
# │ How:     Illustrative epochs in one cycle; the gap is |t3 - t2|.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

class MemoryEpochAlignment:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    t1 = 12.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (tactile array latches force)
    t2 = 18.5 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (camera exposure midpoint)
    t3 = 21.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (encoders sample angles)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    gap = abs(t3 - t2).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t1 < t2 < t3, "The illustrative epochs must be in sampling order.")
    check(abs(gap.magnitude - 2.5) < 1e-9, "Camera-to-encoder gap is 2.5 ms.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    t1_str = fmt_latency(t1, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t2_str = fmt_latency(t2, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t3_str = fmt_latency(t3, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    gap_str = fmt_latency(gap, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Physical systems often combine asynchronously acquired signals, even though hardware triggers can align selected sensors. In an illustrative asynchronous cycle, a tactile array might latch normal force readings at $t_1 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t1_str`, an optical tracking camera might have its exposure midpoint at $t_2 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t2_str`, and joint optical encoders might sample angular positions at $t_3 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t3_str`. These observations occur at different epochs and cannot be combined through direct tensor concatenation or algebraic operations. In multimodal foundation models and vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, visual tokens, proprioceptive vectors, and tactile embeddings are frequently packed into a single attention sequence under the implicit assumption that all tokens capture a simultaneous physical snapshot. However, attending across unaligned sensory tokens without kinematic projection introduces synthetic spatial dislocations into the latent state representation: the attention weights correlate a historical hand position at $t_2$ with an instantaneous joint torque at $t_3$, hallucinating nonexistent contact dynamics. Fusing a camera observation at $t_2$ with an encoder observation at $t_3$ requires the consumer to project one state across the temporal gap $\Delta t = |t_3 - t_2| =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.gap_str` using explicit kinematic models and bounded velocities (for example, propagating the historical camera observation along the joint velocity vector to reconcile it with the instantaneous encoder reading). Without the true acquisition epoch for each individual signal, the alignment calculation cannot determine the sign or magnitude of $\Delta t$, compounding geometric errors across every inference cycle.

With these epochs and the clock-synchronization bound carried in the record of @sec-memory-handoff, the consumer computes the elapsed duration between the evidence epoch and the execution deadline, evaluates the worst-case expansion of the error bound, and determines whether the state remains within task tolerances. Handing over a state without its acquisition epoch leaves the consumer blind to transport delays and scheduling jitter, turning deterministic control into open-loop guesswork. Because physical geometry also changes as bodies move through space, spatial transforms between reference frames are subject to the same temporal decay, carrying their own distinct evidence epochs.

## Coordinate Transform Expiry and Calibration Drift {#sec-memory-reference-frames}

A coordinate frame binds a spatial representation, but in an active physical machine the frame itself moves. In embodied architectures, sensors, chassis links, and end-effectors are related through a directed acyclic transform graph. What the static graph does not show is how an edge goes stale. Each edge of the tree in @fig-09-robot-transform-tree stores a rigid-body pose parameterized by joint angles [@lynch2017modern; @craig2005introduction], and that pose describes the machine only at the epoch when its physical geometry was transduced. When an onboard computer chains transforms measured at different times—due to neural inference latency, transport delay, asynchronous sensor sampling, or dropped frames—the mathematical product is a hybrid pose that the physical machine never occupied (@sec-appendix-control-spatial defines coordinate mapping and transform-chain composition).

In modern spatial attention backbones and 3D foundation models, transforming query coordinates into world space using a stale transform corrupts spatial indexing. When a cross-attention layer projects a query point $\mathbf{x}_{\text{query}}$ via an uncompensated transform $\mathbf{T}_{W \leftarrow C}(t - \Delta t)$, the resulting world coordinates are displaced by the kinematic lever-arm error $\Delta \mathbf{x} \approx \mathbf{J} \Delta \boldsymbol{\theta}$. This spatial mis-indexing causes the cross-attention layers to retrieve keys and values from empty space or neighboring obstacles in the 3D state store, silently corrupting the policy's spatial attention working set. In software execution, every matrix multiplication evaluates cleanly without throwing a runtime exception; the failure manifests silently as an ungrounded attention working set that gathers keys from empty air.

A transform also spans several machine words (six or seven floating-point numbers for translations and rotation quaternions), so a high-rate control reader racing an asynchronous vision writer can observe an old rotation paired with a new translation. The lock-free seqlock mailbox established in @sec-nervous-cadences closes this concurrency race without blocking hard real-time control threads: each reader makes one bounded attempt per tick and never waits; a torn read is discarded, and the last validated transform ages in its place.

::: {#fig-09-robot-transform-tree fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Manipulator kinematic frame tree and temporal dynamics**: Articulated manipulator geometry (a) and corresponding directed acyclic coordinate transform tree in ROS \\texttt{tf2} (b). Each directed edge stores a homogeneous transformation matrix parameterized by joint state. Composing transforms across disparate acquisition epochs injects lever-arm positioning error $e_{\\text{tool}} \\approx \\ell\\,\\Delta\\theta$, while an uncompensated asynchronous edge references stale coordinates (adapted from Craig 2005 and Foote 2013 [@craig2005introduction; @foote2013tf])." fig-alt="Manipulator Kinematic Frame Tree and Temporal Lever-Arm Dynamics. (a) Physical geometry of an articulated manipulator with base link, joint linkages, wrist camera, and tool center point (tool0), indicating lever arm ℓ and angular deflection error e_tool ≈ ℓ · Δθ. (b) Spatial transformation tree (DAG) connecting world reference, base link, kinematic chain link1 through link6, wrist frame, wrist camera, tool0 TCP, and target object, highlighting an asynchronous stale transform edge. (Adapted from Craig 2005 and Foote 2013)."}
![](images/svg/fig09_canonical_robot_frame_tree.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In @fig-09-robot-transform-tree, panel (a) illustrates the physical geometry of an articulated serial manipulator carrying an eye-in-hand wrist camera and an end-effector tool center point (`tool0`). Mechanical links (`link1` through `link6`) are connected by revolute joints whose optical encoders continuously sample joint angles $\theta_i(t)$. The tool tip extends beyond the wrist joint by an effective lever arm $\ell$. When the wrist turns at angular rate $\omega$, any temporal latency $\Delta t$ in the wrist coordinate frame introduces an angular lag $\Delta\theta = \omega\,\Delta t$, sweeping the tool tip across an unmodeled circular arc $e_{\text{tool}} \approx \ell\,\Delta\theta$.

Panel (b) depicts the corresponding coordinate transform tree maintained as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in robot middleware such as ROS `tf2` [@foote2013tf]. Each directed edge represents a $4 \times 4$ homogeneous transformation matrix $\mathbf{T}_{A \leftarrow B}$ mapping points from child frame $B$ into parent frame $A$. Because internal joint encoders publish at high cadences (typically $500\text{--}1{,}000\text{ Hz}$) over deterministic fieldbuses while external visual perception pipelines publish target poses (`target_object`) at camera framerates ($30\text{--}60\text{ Hz}$) over asynchronous network transports, the transform tree inevitably buffers edges with disparate timestamps. If an asynchronous edge (such as `wrist_camera` to `target_object`) drops a frame or stalls, compounding the current robot arm forward kinematics $\mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{wrist}}(t)$ with a stale vision edge $\mathbf{T}_{\text{wrist} \leftarrow \text{object}}(t - \Delta t)$ instantiates the **chimeric kinematic product anti-pattern**\index{Chimeric kinematic product anti-pattern!definition}: synthesizing an unphysical hybrid pose that the robot never occupied.

In robotics middleware like ROS `tf2`, transform listeners resolve coordinate frames by querying the transform tree. Historical queries can interpolate between buffered samples ($t_1 \le t \le t_2$), but a query beyond the latest available sample cannot interpolate into an unobserved future. The **real-time extrapolation dilemma** is therefore an application decision, not a requirement that middleware invent a pose. A lookup can fail immediately when the requested transform is unavailable, or a noncritical caller can wait subject to a timeout. The permission path requires bounded, nonblocking lookup and explicit rejection on failure. An application that instead predicts the transform must carry a validated growth bound; naive extrapolation during a communication stall otherwise accumulates lever-arm error $e_{\text{rot}} \approx \ell\,\omega\,\Delta t$.

The cost of an expired transform is direct spatial displacement (@fig-frame-staleness-error). Applying the age-as-displacement relation of @sec-perception-photons-to-claims to kinematics, uncompensated latency translates directly into geometric positioning error through the lever arm of the linkages. For the rigorous cross-product derivation of this kinematic error propagation, see @sec-appendix-control-spatial.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-latch-transform-staleness
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STALE SLOT-TO-FINGER TRANSFORM AT THE LATCH SLOT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-reference-frames (lever-arm staleness example); owns
# │          the latch-slot constants that @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion
# │          (LatchSlotBelief) reads.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that one missed wrist-camera frame on the slot-to-finger
# │          edge can spend more than the latch-release slot's tolerance, most
# │          of it through the lever arm.
# │ Show:    the frame period, the lateral drift at the finger's drift bound,
# │          the lever-arm arc, and their sum with E0 against the slot.
# │ How:     e_tool ~ E0 + v_drift dt + l omega dt, dt one wrist-camera frame.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LatchTransformStaleness:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    frame_rate = RM.wrist_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet (wrist camera)
    e0 = 0.1 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (finger-to-slot error at the wrist capture)
    v_drift = 12.0 * ureg.millimeter / ureg.second  # category: illustrative (unobserved lateral velocity error bound)
    e_max = 1.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (latch-release slot tolerance)
    lever = 0.15 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (wrist-to-fingertip lever arm)
    omega = 0.30 * ureg.radian / ureg.second  # category: illustrative (wrist rate while aligning the finger)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    dt = (1 / frame_rate).to(millisecond)
    e_trans = (v_drift * dt).to(ureg.millimeter)
    e_rot = (lever * omega * dt / ureg.radian).to(ureg.millimeter)
    e_tool = (e0 + e_trans + e_rot).to(ureg.millimeter)
    ratio = (e_tool / e_max).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dt.magnitude - 16.667) < 1e-3, f"Wrist-camera frame period should be 16.7 ms, got {dt}.")
    check(abs(e_trans.magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-6, f"Lateral drift over one frame should be 0.20 mm, got {e_trans}.")
    check(abs(e_rot.magnitude - 0.75) < 1e-6, f"Lever-arm arc should be 0.75 mm, got {e_rot}.")
    check(e_rot > e_trans, "The lever arm must contribute more than the lateral drift.")
    check(e_tool > e_max, "One missed frame must exceed the slot tolerance.")
    check(abs(e_tool.magnitude - 1.05) < 1e-6, f"Total finger error should be 1.05 mm, got {e_tool}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    dt_str = fmt_latency(dt, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    e0_str = fmt_length(e0, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    v_drift_str = fmt_velocity(v_drift, unit=ureg.millimeter / ureg.second, precision=0)
    lever_str = fmt_length(lever, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    omega_str = fmt_angular_velocity(omega, precision=2)
    e_trans_str = fmt_length(e_trans, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_rot_str = fmt_length(e_rot, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_tool_str = fmt_length(e_tool, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_max_str = fmt_length(e_max, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    ratio_pct_str = fmt_percent(ratio - 1, precision=0, style="prose")
```

How little staleness it takes to spend a task's tolerance shows at the latch-release slot, while the wrist camera can still see it. Each wrist-camera frame, one every `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.dt_str`, renews the slot's pose in the camera frame and with it the slot-to-finger edge the controller aligns on, and the finger must stay within the slot tolerance $E_{\max}$ of `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_max_str`. To isolate the effect of one frame period, suppose the supporting observation is available at its capture epoch, with ingestion delay idealized as zero, and the edge then ages by one frame period. A deployed edge is already older when ingestion completes; its consumer must qualify and charge the full capture-to-use age, including processing, transport, and any additional missed frames. Starting from an initial error of `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e0_str`, the finger's lateral offset drifts at most $e_{\text{trans}} = v_{\text{drift}}\,\Delta t$ under an illustrative `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.v_drift_str` bound on its unobserved lateral velocity, validated for the arm's operating region, or `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_trans_str`. With the fingertip an illustrative $\ell$ = `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.lever_str` beyond the wrist and the wrist turning at an illustrative $\omega$ = `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.omega_str` as it aligns the finger, the lever arm adds $e_{\text{rot}} \approx \ell\,\omega\,\Delta t$, or `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_rot_str`. The joint encoders measure that turn, but the stale edge still dates the slot to the previous frame while the wrist pose it is composed with is current, so the tree returns a hybrid pose, a finger position the arm never held. Only chaining the slot against the wrist pose of its own capture epoch, or expiring the edge, removes that arc. Left in the chain, the stale edge misplaces the finger by `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_tool_str`, `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.ratio_pct_str` more than the slot allows, and more of that error comes from the lever arm than from the drift. Because the transform tree evaluates without error, nothing flags the stale pose, and the controller keeps aligning the finger on a slot position that is off by more than the clearance, which on an unfavorable approach puts the finger against the strike plate beside the slot.

::: {#fig-frame-staleness-error fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Transform staleness and lever-arm error at the latch-release slot**: Illustrative finger error over one frame period, with zero ingestion delay assumed to isolate this contribution. A deployed calculation must use full capture-to-use age. The slot-to-finger edge ages by duration $\\Delta t$. Lateral drift at the velocity bound $v_{\\text{drift}}$ moves the finger by $e_{\\text{trans}} = v_{\\text{drift}}\\,\\Delta t$, while the wrist turning at $\\omega$ swings the fingertip, a lever arm $\\ell$ beyond it, by $e_{\\text{rot}} \\approx \\ell\\,\\omega\\,\\Delta t$. Composing the stale edge with the current wrist pose adds both to the initial error $E_0$, so the finger error $e_{\\text{tool}} \\approx E_0 + e_{\\text{trans}} + \\ell\\,\\Delta\\theta$ exceeds the slot tolerance $E_{\\max}$." fig-alt="Transform staleness at the latch-release slot. A dashed ghost arm shows the wrist and finger as dated by the stale edge at t0, with a dashed circle marking the slot tolerance E_max around the finger. The current arm at t0 + Δt shows the wrist shifted laterally by e_trans = v_drift Δt and the link of length ℓ turned by Δθ = ω Δt, which swings the finger by e_rot ≈ ℓ Δθ. A red vector from the stale finger position to the current finger, labeled e_tool ≈ E_0 + e_trans + ℓ Δθ, ends well outside the E_max circle."}
![](images/svg/fig09_frame_staleness_error.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The red vector in @fig-frame-staleness-error crosses the tolerance boundary even though every matrix multiplication remains valid. The worked calculation locates the dominant error in the wrist's lever arm, so increasing timestamp precision alone would not repair the chain. The consumer must compose compatible epochs or reject the expired edge.

::: {#psp-memory-leverage-of-staleness .callout-perspective title="The leverage of staleness"}
*A transform's admissible age is set at the point it serves, not at the joint it measures. The tool point drifts at roughly $v + \ell\omega$, so the longer the lever arm, the sooner an edge expires, and an edge still fresh enough to locate the wrist can be too old to locate the tool center point.*
:::

A stale transform displaces both the tool estimate and any observations mapped through it. The surrounding world ages too, but it has no joint encoders to report its motion. Memory must therefore record which surfaces and empty regions the sensors actually verified, as well as the frames in which those observations hold.

## Certified Spatial Assertions in Scene Memory {#sec-memory-scene-attention-buffers}

After the robot sweeps its range sensor down an aisle, memory must distinguish space it saw occupied, space it saw empty, and space it never saw. Only observed empty space can support a clearance claim, and only while that evidence remains valid. A map that merges unknown space with free space defeats the evidence-age checks even if every stored timestamp is correct.

The representation must also serve consumers with different needs. A learned policy needs object identity and local geometry to propose a route or grasp. The permission path needs bounded geometric queries whose evidence can be checked before its deadline. Metric maps supply distances and occupancy, scene graphs organize those quantities into objects and places, and episodic memory preserves the interaction history needed to interpret them. These layers share evidence without giving a semantic label or remembered event authority to certify clearance.

### Volumetric metric maps and distance fields {#sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps}

The aisle clearance query needs a conservative distance to occupied or unknown space, together with the evidence supporting that distance. A rendering query asks a different question. Before choosing how to store the scene, we allocate the local collision workload and then compare candidate representations against it. All representation timings and memory densities in the comparison below are illustrative design points, not measurements of the named implementations or qualified worst-case bounds.

#### Collision query latency deadlines for reactive safety filters {.unnumbered}

The worked design allocates spatial collision checking within a $1\text{ kHz}$ permission loop ($T_{\text{tick}} = 1{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$). The required query returns conservative clearance at each body collision hull; where the selected filter needs a gradient, that work belongs in the same measured query. For the illustrative $N_{\text{hulls}} = 20\text{--}50$ evaluation spheres, the total work is:
$$T_{\text{query\_total}} = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\text{hulls}}} t_{\text{query}}(\mathbf{x}_k) \le T_{\text{reflex\_budget}}$$ {#eq-mem-query-latency-budget}
To bound the total collision workload in @eq-mem-query-latency-budget, the worked $N_{\text{hulls}} = 50$ case reserves $T_{\text{reflex\_budget}} = 100\ \mu\text{s}$ for local collision checking, leaving 90 percent of the tick for the other permission and communication work. This is an allocation to be tested on the deployed controller; full-map updates and trajectory optimization run outside this tick. Dividing the allocation among the hulls gives:
$$t_{\text{query}} \le \frac{T_{\text{reflex\_budget}}}{N_{\text{hulls}}} \approx \frac{100\ \mu\text{s}}{50} = 2.0\ \mu\text{s}$$

The resulting per-query allocation selects among the illustrative design points in @fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto. It does not qualify any implementation by itself.

At the stated octree query times, checking the full set consumes more than the entire tick. The neural-field points represent ray-rendering work, so their latency does not measure a clearance lookup. The illustrative ESDF lookup of $0.85\ \mu\text{s}$ gives $42.5\ \mu\text{s}$ for the set, leaving room inside the collision allocation for the remaining checks. This makes the ESDF a candidate for the local snapshot, subject to measured execution time, storage capacity, and conservative treatment of unknown cells. A TSDF's projective distance cannot be substituted for Euclidean clearance merely because its lookup is fast.

The host maintains the larger reconstruction and prepares a bounded region covering the admitted motion and its fallback. The permission controller accepts a snapshot only when its provenance, geometry bounds, per-region evidence ages, and coverage satisfy the qualified interface. Snapshot construction, transfer, and admission consume time and memory of their own; @sec-placement must place and qualify that work separately from the local query. If the host stalls, the existing snapshot keeps aging. Motion can continue only while its own evidence, coverage, and fallback remain valid.

::: {#fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**3D scene representation frontier: memory footprint vs. spatial query latency**: Illustrative design points compare storage density with query-work latency across representation families. Neural-field points describe ray rendering, not clearance lookups, and are excluded from the dashed geometric-query comparison. The workloads are not normalized benchmarks. The green band marks the worked allocation of at most $2\\ \\mu\\text{s}$ per local query. Points inside that band are candidates for qualification, not measured execution guarantees; representation, resolution, query semantics, and hardware must be evaluated together." fig-alt="Log-log scatter plot of volumetric memory footprint in megabytes per cubic meter vs. latency of differing query workloads in microseconds. Neural-field points show rendered-ray latency. Shaded green region highlights the worked local-query allocation at or below 2 us, and shaded red region indicates the deliberative zone above 100 us."}

The logarithmic axes in @fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto expose the capacity–query trade-off for the stipulated comparison. Fast local lookup favors a distance field, while host reconstruction and semantic planning may justify other layers. The choice therefore produces two resource obligations: bounded local queries for permission, and host storage, update, and conversion work to keep that snapshot supplied. The representation mechanisms below determine the second obligation.

#### Representation mechanisms behind the choice {.unnumbered}

The query calculation favors a local distance field for this worked allocation. The following mechanisms explain its storage and update costs, and why the host may retain a different representation for rendering or semantic planning. The quoted densities and timings retain the illustrative status of the comparison; they are not universal properties of these algorithms.

1. **Occupancy Grids and Hierarchical Octrees**: Discretizes 3D space into uniform cubic voxels of side length $r$ [@elfes1989using]. Each voxel cell $m_i$ stores an occupancy probability $P(m_i=1)$, updated recursively via standard log-odds additions.[^fn-math-log-odds] Dense grids scale linearly with workspace volume and cubically with inverse voxel width; allocating a $1\text{ m}^3$ workspace at fine $2\text{ mm}$ resolution requires $(1000/2)^3 = 1.25 \times 10^8$ voxels, consuming $125.0\text{ MB/m}^3$ at 1 byte per voxel. To avoid allocating empty volumes, hierarchical octrees (such as OctoMap [@hornung2013octomap]) group eight sibling voxels recursively, pruning homogeneous free space to achieve compact storage ($0.18\text{--}1.25\text{ MB/m}^3$ at $2\text{--}5\text{ cm}$). However, pointer dereferencing across tree depths introduces CPU cache misses, resulting in query latencies of $24\text{--}38\ \mu\text{s}$.
2. **Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDF)**: Rather than binary occupancy, a TSDF stores the projective distance $d(\mathbf{x})$ from voxel center $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ to the nearest observed surface along the sensor sightline [@curless1996volumetric]. Given camera pose $\mathbf{T}_{C \leftarrow W}$ and depth image $D_{\text{obs}}(\mathbf{u})$, projective distance along the optical axis is $d_k(\mathbf{x}) = D_{\text{obs}}(\pi(\mathbf{T}_{C \leftarrow W}\mathbf{x})) - [\mathbf{T}_{C \leftarrow W}\mathbf{x}]_z$. Normalizing by truncation distance $\delta$ yields $\phi_k(\mathbf{x}) = \text{clamp}(d_k(\mathbf{x})/\delta, -1, 1)$. The voxel state is updated via running weighted average:
$$D_k(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{W_{k-1}(\mathbf{x}) D_{k-1}(\mathbf{x}) + w_k(\mathbf{x}) \phi_k(\mathbf{x})}{W_{k-1}(\mathbf{x}) + w_k(\mathbf{x})}, \quad W_k(\mathbf{x}) = \min(W_{k-1}(\mathbf{x}) + w_k(\mathbf{x}), W_{\max})$$
where $w_k(\mathbf{x}) \propto 1/\sigma_d^2$ weights range precision. Spatial hashing frameworks (such as Voxblox [@oleynikova2017voxblox]) allocate voxel blocks only within the narrow band $[-\delta, +\delta]$ around perceived surfaces, achieving moderate storage ($4.1\text{ MB/m}^3$ at $5\text{ cm}$) and rapid raycasting ($1.8\ \mu\text{s}$).

3. **Euclidean Signed Distance Fields (ESDF)**: While a TSDF measures distance along optical camera rays, motion planning and reactive obstacle avoidance require the true Euclidean distance to the nearest physical obstacle: $d_E(\mathbf{x}) = \min_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{S}} \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|$, with negative signs inside solid geometry. Propagating wave-front expansions across hashed TSDF blocks yields an ESDF. Although maintaining the Euclidean distance field increases memory overhead ($28.5\text{ MB/m}^3$ at $2\text{ cm}$), the illustrative design point assigns $0.85\ \mu\text{s}$ to a distance lookup. Away from the surface, with a unique closest obstacle point, the unsigned exterior distance has gradient $\nabla d_E(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}^*)/\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}^*\|$. Nearest-obstacle ties can make the gradient undefined, and voxel interpolation adds its own approximation. A consumer that needs gradients must qualify those cases rather than assume global smoothness.
4. **3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)**: Parameterizes geometry as an explicit collection of anisotropic 3D Gaussian ellipsoids [@kerbl20233d], each defined by continuous density $G_i(\mathbf{x}) = \exp(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_i)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_i))$, with mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^3$,[^fn-math-gaussian-covariance] opacity $o_i \in [0, 1]$, and spherical harmonics color coefficients $c_i$. Projected to the 2D image plane via viewing transform $\mathbf{W}$ and projection Jacobian $\mathbf{J}$, the 2D covariance is $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i' = \mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{W}^\top\mathbf{J}^\top$. Rasterization accumulates color via front-to-back alpha blending across depth-sorted Gaussians $\mathcal{N}$:
$$C = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}} c_i \alpha_i \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j), \quad \alpha_i = o_i \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_i')^\top (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i')^{-1}(\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_i')\right)$$
For a geometric query, each Gaussian can be enclosed by its $3\sigma$ ellipsoid $(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_i)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_i) \le 9$. This hull describes the fitted Gaussian, not a validated bound on physical surface error or free space. A GPU Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) can index those hulls. The illustrative 3DGS design points pair moderate memory density ($1.6\text{--}5.2\text{ MB/m}^3$) with spatial queries ($5.8\text{--}8.2\ \mu\text{s}$) and view-synthesis capability (@fig-09-3dgs-spatial-memory).

5. **Implicit Neural Representations (NeRF / Coordinate MLPs)**: Encodes volumetric density $\sigma(\mathbf{x})$ and color $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})$ within the stationary weights of a multilayer perceptron (MLP). Synthesizing views evaluates the continuous volume rendering integral along camera ray $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$:
$$C(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f} T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d})\,dt, \quad T(t) = \exp\left(-\int_{t_n}^t \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s))\,ds\right)$$
The illustrative neural-field point pairs a compact density model ($0.08\text{ MB/m}^3$) with a rendered-ray workload ($650\ \mu\text{s}$). Rendering evaluates density and color at multiple quadrature points along a ray. It is not a signed-distance query: a radiance field does not directly supply conservative Euclidean clearance. That use requires a separately constructed and qualified geometric representation, whose query cost must be measured on its own terms.

[^fn-math-log-odds]: **Recursive log-odds occupancy formulation**\index{Occupancy grid!log-odds update}: In binary Bayes filters, occupancy probabilities are converted to log-odds: $L(m_i) = \ln [P(m_i=1)/(1-P(m_i=1))]$. The recursive update given sensor measurement $z_t$ simplifies to addition: $L(m_i \mid z_{1:t}) = L(m_i \mid z_{1:t-1}) + L(m_i \mid z_t) - L_0$, avoiding numerical underflow near 0 and 1.

[^fn-math-gaussian-covariance]: **3D Gaussian covariance parameterization**\index{3D Gaussian Splatting!covariance parameterization}: To guarantee positive semi-definiteness during gradient-based optimization, 3DGS decomposes the spatial covariance matrix into rotation and scaling matrices: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^\top\mathbf{R}^\top \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^3$, where $\mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(s_x, s_y, s_z)$ represents 3D scale radii and $\mathbf{R}$ is a rotation matrix parameterized by a unit quaternion.

::: {#fig-09-3dgs-spatial-memory fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) spatial memory architecture and dual-use pipeline**: (a) Perceptual ingestion: streaming RGB-D frames and camera pose estimates ($T_{W\\_C}$) update the map in real time. (b) Volumetric representation: geometry is explicitly parameterized by anisotropic Gaussian surfels $G(x)$ with learned means $\\boldsymbol{\\mu}$, covariances $\\boldsymbol{\\Sigma}$, and opacities under adaptive density control. (c) Asymmetric systems utilization: rasterizing Gaussians generates photorealistic novel views to service unprivileged deliberative neural planning (top), while a separately qualified conversion supplies conservative local occupancy or distance evidence for the permission gate (bottom). Gaussian hulls alone do not certify clearance; sensor coverage and physical error bounds must support the conversion." fig-alt="Three-panel systems diagram illustrating 3D Gaussian Splatting memory pipeline. Panel (a) shows sensor stream and pose tracking ingestion. Panel (b) shows 3DGS spatial memory with surfels and covariance ellipsoids under adaptive density control. Panel (c) highlights distinct dual uses: rasterization for deliberative planning and conversion to validated occupancy/ESDF for safety permission."}
![](images/svg/fig09_canonical_3dgs_memory.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The local-query decision leaves the host with a capacity and update problem. Keeping the chosen snapshot supplied requires enough memory for the underlying map and enough bandwidth to integrate observations before their evidence expires.

#### Volumetric memory footprint scaling {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-hashed-voxel-payload
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ILLUSTRATIVE HASHED MAP PAYLOAD
# │ Context: @sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps, host capacity calculation.
# │ Goal: Separate voxel payload from total allocated map storage.
# │ Show: Payload for the existing idealized block count, before overhead.
# │ How: blocks × voxels per block × bytes per voxel.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_memory, check

class HashedVoxelPayload:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    blocks = 18_750  # category: illustrative (idealized host-map block count below)
    block_side = 8  # category: illustrative (voxel cells per block edge)
    voxel_bytes = 8 * ureg.byte  # category: illustrative (distance, weight, epoch payload)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    payload = blocks * block_side**3 * voxel_bytes

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(payload.to(ureg.megabyte).magnitude - 76.8) < 1e-9, "Voxel payload is 76.8 MB before overhead.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    payload_str = fmt_memory(payload, unit=ureg.megabyte, precision=1)
```

For the illustrative host-map sizing calculation, consider an operational workspace of physical volume $V_{\text{ws}} = L_x L_y L_z$. Discretizing this domain into cubic voxels of uniform pitch $r$ requires memory proportional to workspace volume and to the inverse cube of voxel width:
$$M_{\text{dense}} = \left(\frac{V_{\text{ws}}}{r^3}\right) S_{\text{voxel}}$$ {#eq-mem-footprint-dense}
where $S_{\text{voxel}}$ represents the storage footprint per voxel (typically 8 bytes: 4 bytes for 32-bit floating-point distance, 2 bytes for observation weight, and 2 bytes for evidence timestamp). Evaluating @eq-mem-footprint-dense for a warehouse workcell of dimensions $10\text{ m} \times 10\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$ ($V_{\text{ws}} = 300\text{ m}^3$) at fine manipulation resolution ($r = 0.01\text{ m}$, or $1\text{ cm}$) demands $(300 / 0.01^3) \times 8\text{ B} = 3 \times 10^8 \times 8\text{ B} = 2.4\text{ GB}$ of static, contiguous DRAM. On an embedded robot computer, dedicating gigabytes of memory purely to an empty uniform voxel array starves parallel vision backbones and real-time controller memory allocations.

Crucially, physical obstacles do not fill three-dimensional space uniformly; they reside on thin two-dimensional surface manifolds embedded in the workspace ($\mathcal{S} \subset \mathbb{R}^3$). Truncating distance fields to a narrow metric band $[-\delta, +\delta]$ around observed surfaces restricts non-trivial distance values to a narrow volumetric shell $V_{\text{band}} \approx 2\delta \cdot A_{\text{surface}}$, where $A_{\text{surface}}$ is the total obstacle surface area. Partitioning space into discrete blocks of $B^3$ voxels (typically $B = 8$, yielding 512 voxels per block) with block physical pitch $L_B = B \cdot r$, the sparse hashed memory footprint obeys:
$$M_{\text{hashed}} = N_{\text{blocks}} \left( B^3 S_{\text{voxel}} + S_{\text{meta}} \right) + N_{\text{buckets}} S_{\text{entry}}$$ {#eq-mem-footprint-hashed}
where $N_{\text{blocks}} \approx \lceil 2\delta A_{\text{surface}} / (B r)^3 \rceil$, $S_{\text{meta}}$ is the block metadata overhead (spatial coordinates, allocation flags), and $S_{\text{entry}}$ is the hash bucket pointer size. Evaluating @eq-mem-footprint-hashed for the same $300\text{ m}^3$ workcell with an obstacle surface area of $A_{\text{surface}} \approx 120\text{ m}^2$ and narrow band $\delta = 4\text{ cm}$, the active surface volume is only $V_{\text{band}} \approx 9.6\text{ m}^3$. The idealized volume estimate gives approximately $N_{\text{blocks}} \approx 18{,}750$ blocks and `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.payload_str` of voxel payload. Total allocation additionally includes block metadata, hash entries, and extra blocks needed to cover surface boundaries; this payload estimate does not establish an upper bound on map memory. That footprint is not an allocation for the isolated permission controller; its local snapshot needs a separate capacity bound.

#### Voxel block hashing index mapping {.unnumbered}

To achieve sparse allocation without incurring the pointer traversal overhead of octrees, modern robotic mapping frameworks [@oleynikova2017voxblox] rely on **voxel block hashing**. Continuous world coordinates $\mathbf{x} = [x, y, z]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3$ are mapped to an integer block index $\mathbf{u} = [u_x, u_y, u_z]^\top \in \mathbb{Z}^3$:
$$\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) = \left\lfloor \frac{\mathbf{x}}{B \cdot r} \right\rfloor$$ {#eq-mem-block-index}
As formulated in @eq-mem-block-index, the continuous world coordinates map to discrete block indices; spatial XOR hashing then resolves $\mathbf{u}$ to an allocated hash table bucket index $h(\mathbf{u}) \in \{0, \dots, N_{\text{buckets}}-1\}$.[^fn-algo-voxel-hashing] Because each 512-voxel block is laid out contiguously in memory ($512 \times 8\text{ B} = 4{,}096\text{ B}$, matching a standard 4 KB OS virtual memory page), spatial block hashing offers expected $O(1)$ block retrieval and improves locality within each block. Hash collisions, cache misses, and concurrent updates still affect latency, so expected complexity cannot replace a measured bound for the local permission query.

[^fn-algo-voxel-hashing]: **Spatial XOR hashing and voxel array offsets**\index{Voxel block hashing!spatial XOR}: Voxel block hashing [@oleynikova2017voxblox] maps integer block coordinates $\mathbf{u} = [u_x, u_y, u_z]^\top$ to bucket index $h(\mathbf{u}) = (u_x \cdot p_1 \oplus u_y \cdot p_2 \oplus u_z \cdot p_3) \bmod N_{\text{buckets}}$ using large prime constants ($p_1=73856093, p_2=19349663, p_3=83492791$). Relative voxel offsets within a block resolve via $\Delta \mathbf{u} = \lfloor \mathbf{x}/r \rfloor - B \mathbf{u}$, mapped to linear memory via $\text{offset} = \Delta u_x + B(\Delta u_y + B\,\Delta u_z)$.

#### DRAM update bandwidth during ray marching {.unnumbered}

When depth cameras stream range frames at framerate $f_{\text{cam}}$ with $N_{\text{rays}} = W \times H$ pixels per frame, updating the volumetric map requires ray marching from the sensor origin to each observed surface point [@curless1996volumetric]. Each ray traverses a line-of-sight distance $d_{\text{ray}}$ at voxel stepping pitch $r$, requiring $N_{\text{steps}} = d_{\text{ray}} / r$ discrete cell evaluations. The raw DRAM update bandwidth consumed by naive ray marching is:
$$\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}} = f_{\text{cam}} \cdot N_{\text{rays}} \cdot \left(\frac{d_{\text{ray}}}{r}\right) \cdot S_{\text{rw}}$$ {#eq-mem-dram-bandwidth}
where $S_{\text{rw}}$ is the read-modify-write memory traffic per traversed voxel (typically 8 to 16 bytes for reading current occupancy/distance, updating running weights, and writing back).

Evaluating @eq-mem-dram-bandwidth for a standard VGA depth stream ($640 \times 480 = 307{,}200$ rays) at $f_{\text{cam}} = 30\text{ Hz}$ ray-marched over an average distance of $d_{\text{ray}} = 2.0\text{ m}$ at resolution $r = 2\text{ cm}$ ($100$ steps per ray):
$$\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}} = 30 \times 307{,}200 \times \left(\frac{2.0}{0.02}\right) \times 8\text{ B} \approx 7.37 \times 10^9\text{ B/s} \approx 7.37\text{ GB/s}$$
On a host system on chip (SoC), these map updates share memory bandwidth with the vision model and other workloads. Their effect depends on access locality and competing traffic, not just peak bandwidth. The update calculation identifies a load to include in the contention test; it does not establish a measured interference bound. Voxel block hashing reduces this traffic by caching active blocks in GPU shared memory or CPU L2 cache and using projective TSDF updates—projecting voxels inside the viewing frustum directly onto the depth image in reverse. These methods reduce repeated memory traffic, but the reduction depends on scene coverage and update strategy. Sparse allocation still grows as the machine explores new regions; a bounded host store needs an explicit retention policy.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_volumetric_raycasting_bandwidth_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical ladder comparing SoC bus limit against dense TSDF and sparse VDB memory bandwidth."}
*Dense voxel updates consume shared memory bandwidth; sparse updates reduce that traffic but still require contention tests.*
:::

What a map can certify comes from how a range return updates it. Traversing the ray from the sensor to the return [@amanatides1987fast], the map asserts **negative evidence**\index{Negative evidence} in every cell the ray crossed and positive evidence in the cell where it ended; @sec-appendix-ml-voxels gives the log-odds update. A valid empty ray can retire a phantom obstacle, but it says nothing about the volume behind a return. A new scan down the aisle therefore cannot renew cells hidden behind the rack. Sparse allocation saves capacity without eliminating ray traversal, and any resulting processing delay adds to evidence age (@sec-placement-resource-contention).

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_active_negative_evidence_chain.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Causal chain showing raycast through free space to surface hit, evicting ghost obstacles."}

*Active negative evidence along sightlines clears phantom obstacles without waiting for timeout decay.*
:::

Because negative evidence renews only the cells a ray crossed, a map's publication time dates none of its cells. The manifest in @tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief therefore carries cell evidence epochs alongside occupancy. For the worked local snapshot, checking a hull includes the supporting cells' evidence and unknown-space status within the allocated query time. A freshly copied distance value with expired source cells cannot establish clearance. The manifest travels with the bounded snapshot as well as the host map; the isolated controller does not traverse the full host store.

For a candidate aisle advance, the local ESDF query returns clearance at a body hull together with the source region supporting it. The consumer evaluates that region at the intended execution time, subtracting the geometric and age-dependent uncertainty from nominal clearance. If the remaining distance covers the hull and required motion margin, this query passes and useful motion remains a candidate for permission. If its nearest limiting region is the occluded cross aisle with expired free-space evidence, the result is unknown; a small numerical distance-query latency cannot rescue the claim. The same representation thus supplies both a useful clearance and an explicit validity decision.

| Map field                                 | Unit or type                         | Meaning and consumer check                                                                      |
|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `voxel_grid_origin`, `voxel_resolution_m` | m; m                                 | Spatial anchor and pitch; match the active frame and calibration                                |
| `map_update_epoch`                        | capture-clock ns                     | Last map publication/update; **not** freshness of every cell                                    |
| `cell_evidence_epoch`                     | capture-clock ns per cell            | Last physical observation for that cell; never refreshed by prediction or unrelated map updates |
| `free_space_sweep_epoch`                  | capture-clock ns per occupancy cell  | Last valid observed free ray through that cell                                                  |
| `clock_conversion`, `sync_error_ns`       | mapping; ns                          | Convert capture epochs to the consumer's monotonic clock with bounded error                     |
| `query_latency_budget_us`                 | $\mu\text{s}$ ($\le 2\ \mu\text{s}$) | Bound collision and distance gradient query time to preserve 1 kHz reactive control loops       |

: **Volumetric belief manifest and cell evidence**: The map header describes layout, query latency budget, and update time, while cell-local acquisition epochs determine whether the particular path region is fresh. The consumer treats unobserved or expired cells as unknown unless a separately validated policy permits traversal. {#tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief tbl-colwidths="[26,22,52]"}

### Hierarchical 3D dynamic scene graphs {#sec-memory-hierarchical-scene-graphs}

Semantic memory sits above the metric layer and inherits its limits. Beyond raw metric volumes and radiance fields, foundation-model-driven physical AI requires spatial memory to organize space into semantic hierarchies. The **3D dynamic scene graph (DSG)**\index{3D dynamic scene graph}, formulated by @rosinol2021kimera in Kimera and extended by @hughes2022hydra in Hydra, bridges continuous 3D-indexed metric state stores with symbolic reasoning by structuring spatial memory into a five-layer hierarchical graph (@fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph):

1. *Metric-Semantic Mesh (Layer 1):* High-resolution triangular mesh capturing fine surface geometry with vertex semantic labels.
2. *Object and Agent Nodes (Layer 2):* Bounded 3D geometric entities with oriented bounding boxes, visual embeddings, and tracked dynamic trajectories.
3. *Places and Freespace Topology (Layer 3):* 3D Voronoi topology and navigable freespace clearance spheres ($p_i$) for planning collision-free paths.
4. *Rooms and Structural Enclosures (Layer 4):* Functional architectural subdivisions partitioned by semantic walls and portals.
5. *Buildings and Global Topology (Layer 5):* Top-level semantic graph governing long-horizon mission allocation.

::: {#fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Hierarchical 3D dynamic scene graph architecture**: Five-layer spatio-temporal memory organization bridging continuous 3D-indexed metric state stores to symbolic foundation reasoning. Layer 1 captures triangular metric mesh geometry; Layer 2 extracts 3D objects and dynamic agents; Layer 3 models topological places via Voronoi freespace clearance spheres ($p_i$); Layer 4 structures architectural rooms and portals; and Layer 5 establishes global building mission topology. Vertical inter-layer edges coordinate upward abstraction (compressing metric surfaces into symbolic entities) and downward grounding (translating task tokens into metric coordinates) (adapted from Rosinol et al. [@rosinol2021kimera] and Hughes et al. [@hughes2022hydra])." fig-alt="Hierarchical five-layer 3D Dynamic Scene Graph architecture. From bottom to top: Layer 1 Metric Mesh surface geometry, Layer 2 Objects and Agents with support relations, Layer 3 Places with Voronoi freespace clearance spheres, Layer 4 Rooms connected by portals, and Layer 5 Buildings with global topology. Side arrows depict upward Abstraction and downward Grounding across tiers."}
![](images/svg/fig09_dynamic_scene_graph_hierarchy.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The inter-layer edges in @fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph let a policy reason over objects and places without repeatedly processing the full metric mesh. In the opposite direction, a request for the latch handle resolves through the graph to an object frame and the geometry needed for a candidate approach. Abstraction reduces the working set, but a semantic route still depends on the underlying free-space evidence. A room or object label cannot renew the age of the metric cells beneath it.

### Episodic memory and physical interaction history {#sec-memory-episodic}

While metric voxel grids and dynamic scene graphs maintain spatial persistence—answering *where* objects and free space exist—physical AI agents require **episodic memory**\index{Episodic memory} to record causal history: answering *what happened*, *when it occurred*, and *what physical consequences resulted*. Rather than acting as a passive diagnostic flight recorder or write-only disk log, episodic memory functions as an active, queryable index structured around hybrid automaton transitions, contact events, and tool engagements across multi-minute task horizons.

An episodic memory store in physical AI is structured around three foundational primitives:

1. **Multimodal Interaction Traces**: An episodic trace records an immutable, time-indexed stream of state-action tuples $\tau_k = (t_k, \mathbf{s}_k, \mathbf{a}_k, \mathbf{o}_k, \mathbf{w}_k)$, where $t_k$ is the monotonic capture epoch, $\mathbf{s}_k$ is the estimated kinematic state, $\mathbf{a}_k$ is the executed actuator command, $\mathbf{o}_k$ is the visual observation snapshot, and $\mathbf{w}_k = (\mathbf{f}_k, \boldsymbol{\tau}_k) \in \mathbb{R}^6$ is the high-bandwidth contact wrench measured at the wrist force-torque sensor. Recording wrench signatures alongside kinematic trajectories allows the agent to diagnose unobservable failures (such as slippage, micro-collisions, or latch binding) that leave no trace in visual scene memory.
2. **Action-Event Anchors**: Storing uninterrupted high-frequency telemetry ($1\text{ kHz}$ wrench data and $30\text{ Hz}$ video) rapidly exhausts edge LPDDR5 bandwidth and NVMe storage. Episodic memory manages this deluge by segmenting continuous execution into discrete *action-event anchors*. An anchor is instantiated whenever the physical interaction state experiences a discrete hybrid automaton transition: a sudden rise in normal contact force ($F_n > F_{\text{contact}}$), a gripper switch state change, an unexpected velocity stall ($\|\dot{\mathbf{q}}\| \approx 0$ under active motor effort), or a human operator intervention. Each anchor retains high-resolution telemetry in a localized temporal buffer ($[-500\text{ ms}, +500\text{ ms}]$) around the transition while compressing steady-state transit into low-frequency summary vectors.
3. **Keyframe Context Eviction and Freshness Decay**: When an autoregressive policy or deliberative agent conditions on prior episodic history, its attention context length is strictly bounded by hardware memory limits. In classical NLP, streaming attention evicts older tokens via sliding-window FIFO buffers [@xiao2024streamingllm]. In physical AI, however, FIFO eviction is hazardous: a naive FIFO policy evicts the critical visual observation of a closed latch or a colleague entering a blind aisle simply because dozens of intervening navigation steps consumed the context budget. Physical episodic memory instead implements **saliency-weighted keyframe retention**: event anchors marking mechanical state transitions are pinned to non-volatile belief slots with explicit evidence epochs, while repetitive geometric observations are evicted as fresh metric returns renew the local voxel map.

By decoupling spatial geometry (held in metric TSDF/ESDF layers) from causal interaction history (held in episodic action-event anchors), physical AI systems preserve both the metric clearances needed for immediate collision avoidance and the temporal provenance required for long-horizon task recovery.

A learned policy can retrieve this history without making its context the authoritative state store. A **streaming window**\index{Streaming ring-buffer attention} bounds attention storage by evicting older tokens [@xiao2024streamingllm], whether or not their physical consequences have ended. The metric record and event anchors must therefore outlive context eviction when they still constrain the task. Retrieval gives the policy relevant geometry and history; the Scene Memory State record supplies the evidence age and bound that a motion consumer can check.

For motion permission, then, a representation without an epoch is an unverified assertion, and an estimate whose error bound exceeds task tolerance must be excluded from motion proposals before the permission path considers actuator commands. The machine cannot halt every operation at the first missed frame, however. Extending action across brief sensing gaps requires estimators that propagate belief forward until new measurements arrive to confirm or correct the state.

## Forward State Propagation and Occlusion Decay {#sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion}

When a sensor loses sight of a moving body, stopping also takes time and requires a usable state estimate. Forward propagation carries the last observation across that interval, whether the machine continues a permitted task or executes a fallback. While a learned generative policy might predict future trajectories autoregressively\index{Network!autoregressive}, an ungrounded neural rollout hallucinates smooth continuations without tracking epistemic uncertainty. In physical AI, forward propagation must be coupled to explicit error-growth models—whether implemented via recursive continuous-discrete Kalman filters [@kalman1960new], learned stochastic state observers, or expanding 3D Gaussian covariance ellipsoids.[^fn-hist-bayesian-filter]

Forward propagation changes the estimate and its uncertainty while preserving the hardware evidence epoch. Across the blind interval, anticipated motion remains useful only while the growing error fits the task's clearance. The rack-end example makes that limit explicit.

[^fn-hist-bayesian-filter]: **Bayesian state estimation provenance**\index{State estimation!Bayesian provenance}: @kalman1960new introduced recursive minimum mean-square error state estimation for linear dynamic systems. @moravec1985high generalized these recursive Bayesian updates to spatial occupancy grids, modeling sensor beam uncertainty through explicit range-bearing distributions. In embodied systems, uncompensated propagation across extended sensor dropouts causes Bayesian belief distributions to disperse, requiring explicit invalidation horizons to prevent open-loop control divergence.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-rack-end-belief
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RACK-END BELIEF THROUGH OCCLUSION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion (rack-end belief expiry,
# │          the walking-person term, worked roots, the expiry table, the
# │          skewed-record pitfall), @sec-memory-summary (expiry is physical).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that memory cannot certify an occluded rack end as clear, so
# │          the stopping budget protects only a static obstacle.
# │ Show:    belief expiry against the navigation camera's frame period and
# │          observation age; the running total memory leaves unchanged; the
# │          walking-person term at the drive limit against the clear distance.
# │ How:     Linear growth e(t) = delta_loc + v_h t against delta_margin; the
# │          running total from the RM/AISLE terms at the drive limit; the
# │          walking term v_h (tau_delay + v / a_brake) for a constant-
# │          deceleration stop at the drive limit (the C2 suffix is Ch11's, and
# │          the speed ceiling this term implies is computed in Ch12).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class RackEndBelief:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative (initial error of the belief)
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen (tolerance of the belief)
    v_h = AISLE.v_human_approach  # category: datasheet (ISO 13855 walking speed)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    frame_rate = RM.nav_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet (navigation camera)
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived (@sec-perception-transduction-calibration)
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible deceleration)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (total pre-brake delay)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_exp = ((delta_margin - delta_loc) / v_h).to(millisecond)
    frame_period = (1 / frame_rate).to(millisecond)

    # rows 1-5 of the stopping budget at the drive limit (Ch2, Ch4, Ch8 terms)
    running_total = calc_safe_stopping_distance(
        v_drive,
        AISLE.t_brake_onset + AISLE.t_lease + AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + t_age,
        a_brake,
        delta_loc,
        delta_margin,
    ).to(ureg.millimeter)
```
